name: NuVIE
dek: A watch-tracking app built around deciding what to watch next.

at_a_glance.role: Sole UX/UI designer, end to end
at_a_glance.scope: Competitor analysis, user flows, design system, hi-fi UI, usability testing
at_a_glance.hard_part: Turning an open-ended catalog into a short guided path, so a person with decision fatigue lands on one confident pick instead of endless scrolling.
at_a_glance.look_for: How the mood questionnaire, mode picker, and folder-based watchlists all push toward the same goal: fewer options on screen at any moment.

problem.claim_h2: The problem is not finding movies. It is choosing one.
problem.thesis: Tracking apps tell you where a title streams, but none of them help you decide what to actually watch tonight.
problem.body: A review of Reelgood, JustWatch, Trakt, and IMDb-style recommendation feeds showed the same pattern: passive lists, generic suggestions, and walls of options that make the choice harder. NuVIE reframes the tracker as a decision tool, pairing watchlists and streaming availability with a short mood-based questionnaire.
bullets: Recommendations are trend-driven rather than mood-driven, so they feel generic and impersonal.
Availability tools answer where to watch but leave the harder what-to-watch question open.
Oversized catalogs and cluttered layouts overwhelm exactly the users who want a quick answer.
problem.research_note: A competitor teardown of IMDb, JustWatch, Reelgood, and Trakt compared watchlist handling, streaming info, and recommendation style to locate the gap NuVIE fills.

design.claim_h2: A guided path from mood to one good pick
design.intro: Every screen narrows the decision: pick a mode, answer a few playful questions, get a short list, then track what you saved and watched.

figures.caption: The mode picker leads with occasions, Movie Night or Binge Week, so the first choice is about intent, not titles.
figures.alt: Phone on a dark desk showing NuVIE's orange mode-select screen with Movie Night and Binge Week buttons plus Quick Mode and Advanced Mode options.

figures.caption: Onboarding folds genre selection into signup, so the first recommendation set has taste data before the home screen loads.
figures.alt: Four orange onboarding screens: login, signup with Google, Facebook and Apple options, a favorite-genre picker grid, and a confirmation screen.

figures.caption: One answer per card, one question per screen. The questionnaire replaces catalog scrolling with a short guided quiz that ends in a results grid.
figures.alt: Four screens showing the home feed grouped by Netflix, Hulu and HBO Max, the mode picker, a mood question with four answer cards, and a results grid.

figures.caption: Detail pages surface streaming logos and watch progress inline, and favorites split into user-named folders like Weekend Watchlist.
figures.alt: Movie detail screen with platform logos, rating and episode chips, next to a Favorite List screen organized into Weekend Watchlist and Horror folders with watched-percentage badges.

validation.honest_line: Scenario-based sessions checked whether the recommendation flow, streaming links, and favorite folders were discoverable and intuitive; as a concept prototype, they could not measure whether guided picks beat browsing over real weeks of use.

appendix.framing: Selected system artifacts behind the screens. The component sheet shows the questionnaire and navigation states that carry the guided flow.

figures.caption: Empty and selected states for answer cards, five nav-bar states, and streaming-platform cards define the questionnaire's building blocks.
figures.alt: Component sheet showing navigation bar variants, toggles, question cards in empty and selected states, keyboards, and streaming platform logo cards.
